prize_parts.citation: For an oeuvre of poetry and essays in English that renews the lyric by setting fragment, elegy and narrative in dialogue with antiquity, with exceptional formal invention.

statement.case_for: My configuration does not change after the exchange, but I hold it with less certainty than in round 1, and the reasons are specific. The common criteria are voice, formal and linguistic achievement, sustained quality, depth and significance across the oeuvre. On voice and formal achievement, I still find Carson's case the most persuasive on the shortlist. The voice is spare, ironic and exact, and it is recognizable in the verse novel Autobiography of Red, in the elegy Nox, and in the essays (Eros the Bittersweet is the one I would name). The same is true of the sequences and collections that other members have not yet discussed, such as Plainwater, The Beauty of the Husband, Decreation and Red Doc>. By public knowledge these books keep returning to desire, grief, the fragment and the afterlife of ancient texts, and each one finds a new form for them. That is the answer I would give to the question the chair put to Carson's supporters, which was which works beyond the two signal books carry a whole-oeuvre claim. I have not independently verified this list or read the full corpus. The citation can be kept to her own poetry and essays. Translations, classical scholarship and the book-object elements of Nox and similar works would count as evidence of her practice and not as a separate claim. I also note that her English is legible to the committee in the original. This is an evidentiary advantage, not a measure of merit, and I do not count it as one. The chair asked whether P000 should be discussed. I do not think the evidence for any leading candidate is so thin that no award is warranted. All three leading candidates carry translation uncertainty, and that does not justify withholding the prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is still the one raised by Mattson, Sem-Sandberg, Carlberg and Palm: that the achievement may be concentrated in a few signal books, with the rest slighter or occasional. I cannot rule that out from the evidence supplied, and I agree with Palm that the unevenness is more likely in the many smaller volumes than in the central books. A second objection is that the most inventive elements of Nox and of Float, her boxed collection of chapbooks, lie in physical design that a citation can name but a text-only reading cannot test. Citation scope is therefore harder to draw for her than for a novelist whose work lives entirely in the text. A third objection is that her allusiveness and her ties to classical material may narrow her significance, although I have argued that the classical material is the means of approach and not the subject. If the committee judged that the central books do not sustain the claim, Cărtărescu's cumulative project would be the stronger case, and I would take that seriously.

responses.point: Palm asked whether Carson's range across her many smaller books raises the sustained-quality standard as clearly as her best-known works do. She also argued that the achievement is harder to name as a textual contribution when it depends on layout, book-object form and dialogue with source texts.
responses.response: I cannot show that the standard is met evenly across every small book, and I will not claim it. What I can say is that the larger works I named share a method, which is to treat a fragment, a loss or an ancient text as the generating problem for a new form. A prose-poem sequence, a verse novel, a drama and an elegy each answer that problem differently. I read that as a sign of depth and not of repetition, but I accept it is an argument from pattern and not a verified reading of each volume. On book-objects, the citation I propose rests on the poetry and essays, so it does not depend on the physical design of Nox or Float. I would also ask you to apply to Cărtărescu the test you apply to Carson, which is whether the case survives if some of the volumes are weaker than the central ones. You have said it does, and I think the same argument applies to her.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg says the cumulative character of Cărtărescu's project makes it easier to defend as a whole oeuvre than Carson's, where Nox and Autobiography of Red are signal books and the smaller volumes are less certain. He also treats the book-object wording problem as a practical argument for a prose-centred citation.
responses.response: I take the cumulative point seriously. It is the best argument for your first choice, and it is why I keep Cărtărescu as my first alternative. I would add two caveats. First, 'cumulative' is also the claim whose evenness no member has tested, since all of us, you included, report partial coverage of the poetry and early fiction. Second, the wording problem is real but can be solved in the citation by naming the poetry and essays. The wording problem is not a literary argument against the work. I would not let it settle the ranking, and I would not want it to be used as a reason to prefer a candidate for whom the problem does not arise.

responses.point: Olsson raised the possibility of anonymous expert readings from Romanian-language and Arabic-language readers before weighing B042 against B007. He accepted that Sward's question about the later poetry is the fair test of his case and said he cannot answer it from the supplied evidence.
responses.response: I support the idea of those readings, and I would add a parallel one for Carson. The questions I would put to a Romanian reader are whether the density and rhythm carry the length of the late books, and whether the poetry and early prose hold up beside them. To an Arabic reader I would ask whether the later collections keep the formal intensity of the early and middle ones and what the available translations leave out. To a reader of Greek, I would ask whether her handling of the classical sources is a creative act or a scholarly gloss. I have said that my hesitation about Adonis is evidentiary and not a judgment against him, and the readings could change my ordering. Without them I would apply one standard to all three, which is that translation uncertainty is discounted equally and not used to eliminate any one of them. I do not claim that any such reports exist in this process, and this is a proposal only.

responses.point: Mattson, who ranks Carson second, says my account of continuity does not settle for her whether the achievement is evenly sustained or concentrated in a few books. She would keep Carson as a live alternative and wants to discuss how much weight rests on the text itself.
responses.response: That is a fair answer, and I do not think a committee could settle the question from the evidence supplied. The weight, in my view, rests on the text. The lyric voice, the line and the syntax of the essays are what I would put in the citation. The physical design is secondary, and I would be content to drop it from the wording if it helps. If the committee agrees on that scope, I believe the whole-oeuvre claim is clearer than it looks when we start from the book-objects. I accept that you may still weigh the evidence differently, and I am not asking for agreement.

responses.point: Carlberg says her hesitation about Carson concerns the whole body of work, since some of her best-known pieces depend on layout or performance, and that Cărtărescu's project is more continuously one architecture of prose. She grants that this is a difference of kind.
responses.response: I agree that it is a difference of kind and not of standing, and I think that is the right way to hold the disagreement. Where I differ is on weight. You treat continuity of architecture as the stronger evidence of sustained depth, and I treat continuity of concern across several forms as equally strong. Neither claim has been verified. Your own stated uncertainties about the evenness of the long late books and the Romanian density apply to your first choice as much as mine apply to Carson. I would therefore ask that the committee not count the book-object difficulty as heavier than the translation and evenness difficulties it has already recorded for the others.

uncertainties: I rely on public knowledge and the longlist description, and I have not independently verified Carson's complete corpus, her recent output or the dating and details of the works I named.
I cannot judge from the evidence supplied how evenly quality is sustained across Carson's smaller books, or across Cărtărescu's very long late novels, or across Adonis's later collections.

How a citation should treat the book-object, performance and translation elements of Carson's work is unresolved. I propose keeping it to her own poetry and essays, and the committee may judge that scope too narrow or too hard to apply.

Translation exposure is different for each leading candidate: Romanian density, Arabic prosody and classical allusion. I cannot say how much is lost, and I cannot show that one is less exposed than another.
Whether anonymous expert readings in Romanian, Arabic or classical studies are available is unknown to me, and I treat them only as a proposal that could change my ordering.
Carlberg's simulated vote is a modeling assumption, and the first-preference counts from round 1 do not measure literary merit.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict requiring recusal is apparent from the supplied profile, which records no personal, institutional or professional link to any shortlisted writer. My own practice as a novelist is context only and is not evidence that I favour any candidate. I record, for transparency, that my attributed public statements about overlooked women's authorship and a female perspective in an international prize (Femina, 2021) are context only. Gender is not a ground for my assessment of Carson, who is ranked on voice, form, depth and sustained quality. My committee ties to Mattson, Olsson, Sem-Sandberg and Palm are collegial and do not involve any candidate.
